column1: # Local additions to the vendored word list, in the same TSV format:
# Lines starting with '#' and blank lines are ignored.
# Entries here override words.tsv when keys collide.
# Keep to spellings that are unambiguously wrong in American technical prose.
# Do not add register/dialect swaps that change meaning or tone.
# DO NOT EXTEND THIS LIST BY SUFFIX RULE. Add words one at a time, by hand.
# A suffix rule looks cheaper than a curated list and is not. Most of what it
# matches is not a dialect choice at all. In one US-authored technical corpus,
# 569 of 577 -lled/-lling matches were words whose stem already ends in -ll
# (call, drill, install), and 176 of 324 -ise matches were stem-internal
# (raise, noise), with another 51 being -wise adverbs. Those classes are
# mechanically excludable, and a competent rule would exclude them.
# What remains is not excludable. `controlled` and `labelled` are the same
# orthographic shape with opposite answers: American doubles the l only when
# the final syllable is stressed, so conTROLLED is correct in both dialects
# while LAbelled is British and becomes labeled. The discriminator is stress
# placement, which no rule over letters can see. The residue is also where the
# true positives live -- `mislabelled` is in it.
# This list encodes 177 such stress judgments. That is what it is for: to
# record the calls a rule cannot make.
# On the numbers: the counts above are one author, one technical domain, and
# describe what a NAIVE rule does to a US-authored corpus -- do not quote them
# as a general result. In UK-authored text the -ise class would be thick with
# randomised, organised, characterised and a rule would have real signal there.
# What does generalize is the mechanism, and it is register-independent: a
# suffix rule is dominated by classes that are not dialect choices, and once
# those are excluded the residue turns on stress and etymology rather than
# The one rule that is safe is the prefix resolution in the script, and only
# because it composes a KNOWN-good pair with a prefix: the etymology question
# is already settled by a human having put the stem on the list.
